t: Closest Subsequence Sum - Meet in the Middle
o: We may drop any elements of `nums` (possibly none or all) and want a subset sum minimizing `abs(sum - goal)`. Example 1: `[5,-7,3,5]` itself sums to 6 = goal, so the gap is 0. Example 2: nothing hits -5 exactly; `[7,-9,-2]` sums to -4 and misses by 1, which is provably minimal. Example 3 reminds us the empty subsequence is legal: with all-positive `[1,2,3]` the smallest reachable sum is 0, so the best gap is |-7| = 7. The constraints carry the real signal: n <= 40 makes enumerating all 2^40 subsets (~10^12) hopeless, yet splitting the array into halves of ~20 leaves about a million sums per side - the textbook meet-in-the-middle regime. Negative values also rule out DP indexed by sum, pushing us toward explicit enumeration plus sorting and binary search.
k: n <= 40 is the signature of meet in the middle: two halves of ~20 elements hold at most 2^20 (about a million) subset sums each.
Sort one half's sums; for every sum s of the other half, binary-search goal - s and inspect both neighbors around the insertion point.
Negativity rules out array-indexed subset-sum DP; sorted lists plus binary search stay value-agnostic.
Always seed the enumeration with the empty subsequence (sum 0).

a.i: Start from the single sum 0 and fold in each element x by appending s+x for every sum s already collected - after all n elements the list contains every achievable subsequence sum, so a linear scan for the closest value finishes the job. This direct method is wonderfully short and obviously correct, but the collection doubles per element, so it is practical only for n up to roughly 25.
s: Initialize the list of sums as [0] (the empty subsequence).
For each number, extend the list with (old sum + number) for every old sum.
Return the minimum abs(sum - goal) over all sums.
a.t: O(2^n * n) time - each of the n doublings rebuilds the list; hopeless at n = 40, viable for n <= ~24.
a.sp: O(2^n) space to hold every subset sum.

a.i: Split nums into halves A and B of nearly equal size and enumerate subset sums of each independently - about 2^20 values apiece when n = 40. Every full-subset sum factors as one A-sum plus one B-sum, so fixing a right sum r reduces the task to finding the left sum nearest to goal - r. Sorting the right list once turns each query into a binary search whose bracketing neighbors cover targets falling between two sums.
s: Generate all subset sums of the left half and the right half (each list seeded with 0).
For each left sum s, compute need = goal - s and binary-search it in the right list.
Update the answer with |s + right[idx] - goal| and, if idx > 0, |s + right[idx-1] - goal|.
a.t: O(2^(n/2) * n) time - generating and handling ~2^20 sums per half dominates; sorting adds a matching log factor.
a.sp: O(2^(n/2)) space for the two sum lists.

w: Say 'meet in the middle' early - recognizing that n <= 40 secretly means 2^20-per-half is most of the credit. Pitfalls: forgetting the empty subsequence (seed generators with 0), checking only one side of the binary-search insertion point, and silent overflow in C++/Java (subset sums reach +-4*10^8 and goals +-10^9, so keep 64-bit intermediates). Follow-ups: report the achieving subset (carry bitmasks alongside sums), LC 2035 'Partition Array Into Two Arrays to Minimize Sum Difference' which reuses this exact machinery, and how the story changes when all values are small and non-negative (bitset knapsack).
